content: 1. The interaction affects the conversion of the prodrug mycophenolate mofetil into its active form, mycophenolic acid. However, the enteric-coated formulation of mycophenolate sodium is less sensitive to this interaction. 2. Pantoprazole reduces the levels of nelfinavir through an unspecified mechanism, likely involving CYP2C19 inhibition and decreased gastric pH, which impairs nelfinavir absorption. This coadministration is contraindicated as it may lead to loss of virologic response and resistance development. 3. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of neratinib by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 4. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of nilotinib by increasing gastric pH. Nilotinib’s solubility is pH-dependent and decreases at higher pH levels. Separating doses may not mitigate this effect due to the prolonged action of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs). Avoid or use an alternative drug. 5. Pantoprazole increases the levels or effects of nisoldipine by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 6. Otesaconazole increases the levels or effects of pantoprazole by inhibiting breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP). Use the lowest starting dose of BCRP substrates or consider reducing their dose. Monitor closely. 7. Oxcarbazepine decreases the levels or effects of pantoprazole by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. The net effect of pantoprazole action is unclear due to opposing effects by CYP450 enzymes. Monitor closely. 8. Pantoprazole increases the toxicity of ozanimod by inhibiting BCRP, leading to increased exposure to ozanimod’s active metabolites. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 9. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of pazopanib by increasing gastric pH. Avoid coadministration with drugs that raise gastric pH. Consider using short-acting antacids instead of PPIs or H2 antagonists, and separate antacid and pazopanib dosing by several hours. 10. Pentobarbital decreases the levels or effects of pantoprazole by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. The significance of this interaction is unknown. Monitor closely. 11. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of pexidartinib by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Avoid coadministration of PPIs with pexidartinib. Use H2-receptor antagonists or antacids if needed, and adjust the timing of administration accordingly. 12. Phenobarbital decreases the levels or effects of pantoprazole by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. The significance of this interaction is unknown. Monitor closely. 13. Phenytoin decreases the levels or effects of pantoprazole by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 14. Pantoprazole decreases the levels of phytoestrogens by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The significance of this interaction is unknown. Monitor closely. 15. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of polysaccharide iron by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution and monitor closely. 16. Pantoprazole decreases the levels of ponatinib by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The significance of this interaction is unknown. Monitor closely. 17. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of posaconazole by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution and monitor closely. 18. Regorafenib increases the levels or effects of pantoprazole by inhibiting BCRP. Coadministration with a BCRP substrate may increase systemic exposure and related toxicity. Monitor closely. 19. Rifampin decreases the levels or effects of pantoprazole by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 20. Pantoprazole decreases the levels of rilpivirine by increasing gastric pH. This coadministration is contraindicated as it may cause treatment failure and resistance development. 21. Pantoprazole increases the levels or effects of riociguat by decreasing its metabolism. Avoid or use an alternative drug. Monitor for signs of hypotension and adjust the dose if needed. 22. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of rose hips by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution and monitor closely. 23. Rucaparib increases the levels or effects of pantoprazole by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism. Adjust the dosage of CYP2C19 substrates if clinically indicated. Monitor closely. 24. Safinamide increases the levels or effects of pantoprazole by inhibiting intestinal BCRP. Monitor BCRP substrates for increased pharmacologic or adverse effects. Use caution and monitor closely. 25. Concomitant use of PPIs with secretin may cause a hyperresponse in gastrin secretion during stimulation testing, falsely suggesting gastrinoma. Elevated gastrin levels return to normal within three months after discontinuing short-term pantoprazole therapy. 26. Pantoprazole increases the levels or effects of selexipag by inhibiting BCRP. Monitor selexipag for increased pharmacologic or adverse effects when coadministered with BCRP inhibitors. 27. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir by increasing gastric pH. Velpatasvir’s solubility decreases as gastric pH increases. Avoid coadministration with PPIs. If necessary, administer sofosbuvir/velpatasvir with food four hours before omeprazole 20 mg. 28. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of sotorasib by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. If coadministration with acid-reducing agents cannot be avoided, administer sotorasib four hours before or ten hours after a locally-acting antacid. 29. Sparsentan decreases the levels or effects of pantoprazole by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. PPIs may reduce sparsentan exposure, potentially reducing its efficacy. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 30. St. John’s Wort decreases the levels or effects of pantoprazole by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 31. Stiripentol increases the levels or effects of pantoprazole by inhibiting BCRP. Consider dosage reduction for BCRP substrates if adverse effects occur. Monitor closely. 32. Pantoprazole increases the levels or effects of tacrolimus by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism. Concomitant administration may increase tacrolimus concentrations, particularly in intermediate or poor CYP2C19 metabolizers. Use caution and monitor closely. 33. Tafamidis increases the levels or effects of pantoprazole by inhibiting BCRP. Dosage adjustment of BCRP substrates may be necessary. Monitor closely. 34. Pantoprazole increases the levels or effects of talazoparib by inhibiting BCRP. Avoid or use an alternative drug. If coadministration cannot be avoided, monitor for potential adverse reactions. 35. Tecovirimat increases the levels or effects of pantoprazole by inhibiting CYP2C19. Monitor for adverse effects if coadministered with sensitive substrates of these enzymes. 36. Pantoprazole increases the toxicity of theophylline due to prolonged hypochlorhydria, which alters intestinal motility. Monitor for toxicity. 37. Pantoprazole decreases the levels of thyroid desiccated by increasing gastric pH. Conflicting evidence exists regarding this interaction. Monitor closely. 38. Triclabendazole increases the levels or effects of pantoprazole by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 39. Vadadustat increases the levels or effects of pantoprazole by inhibiting BCRP. Monitor for signs of adverse effects of BCRP substrates and adjust their dose as needed. 40. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of vismodegib by altering its solubility due to increased gastric pH. The effect on efficacy is unknown. Use caution and monitor closely. 41. Voriconazole increases the levels or effects of pantoprazole by affecting CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 42. Long-term PPI use may lead to malabsorption or deficiency of cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12). Acute interstitial nephritis has been reported in patients taking PPIs. Discontinue therapy and evaluate patients with suspected acute interstitial nephritis. 43. Relief of symptoms does not eliminate the possibility of gastric malignancy. Consider additional follow-up and diagnostic testing in patients with suboptimal response or early symptomatic relapse after completing PPI treatment. 44. PPI use is associated with an increased risk of Salmonella and Campylobacter infections. 45. PPIs may elevate and/or prolong serum concentrations of methotrexate and its metabolite, potentially leading to toxicity. Consider temporary withdrawal of PPI therapy during high-dose methotrexate administration. 46. PPI therapy is associated with an increased risk of fundic gland polyps, particularly with long-term use exceeding one year. Use the shortest duration of therapy appropriate for the condition being treated. 47. Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN) has been reported in patients taking PPIs. Discontinue therapy and evaluate patients with suspected acute TIN. 48. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Advise pregnant women of the potential risk of fetal harm. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. 49. Pantoprazole and its metabolites are excreted in rat milk. Pantoprazole excretion in human milk has been detected in a study of a single nursing mother. Based on the potential for tumorigenicity shown in rodent studies, decide whether to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering the benefit of the drug to the mother. 50. Pantoprazole is generally acceptable for use during pregnancy. Controlled studies in pregnant women show no evidence of fetal risk. 51. When administered through a Y-site, immediately stop use if precipitation or discoloration occurs.
